newsitem.title: USA: Steady U.S. rates seen neutral factor for markets.
newsitem.headline: Steady U.S. rates seen neutral factor for markets.

text.p: Unchanged Federal Reserve monetary policy will not lend any support to U.S. financial markets or the dollar, analysts said on Tuesday.
The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) left the federal funds rate unchanged at 5.50 percent, as unanimously forecast by Fed watchers.

"This was so widely expected, it won't help the Treasury market," said deputy chief economist Carol Stone at Nomura Securities International Inc. "The bond market is doing the Fed's work and it will continue to do, reacting to economic numbers, as it has done so already for a while."

The 30-year Treasury bond erased earlier modest gains following news at 1415 EDT/1815 GMT that the FOMC meeting had ended without a rate change announcement. Other Treasury prices slipped into negative territory.
U.S. stocks slid in sympathy, with the Dow Jones Industrial Average tumbling from a 100-point-plus rise.
Dollar/mark also retreated below the 1.84 level.

"More analysts are coming around to the notion that the Fed is unlikely to do anything in September either," Stone said. "This gives bond traders an opportunity to think for themselves. The market will analyze each report."
The FOMC has three more scheduled meetings this year: on September 30, November 12 and December 16.
Wrightson and Associates chief economist Lou Crandall said the Fed has adopted a pragmatist approach to monetary policy that is essentially based on the good inflation performance.
Crandall did not expect the Fed to move unless some inflationary signs surface.
"There is no room for Fed policy to be conducted without the facts," said the Wrightson economist, who noted the absence of market reaction to the much-anticipated absence of a funds rate hike.

"Even if the Fed saw a reason for tightening, politically, it would be impossible for them to do so unless you have more tangible evidence of inflation pressures," Crandall added. "In the face of inflation data as positive as those that we have seen, theory alone is not enough to justify a tightening in a political sense."
The Fed came under criticism from lawmakers of both parties as well as from labor and corporate America for raising rates in March by a modest 25 basis points.
This was the first such move in more than two years and only the ninth hike since the expansion started in 1991.
"It's an event (the Fed) that you had to get out of the way in order to go on with your business," said Kevin Harris, senior currency analyst at MCM CurrencyWatch.

"We have a lot more important things coming up for the dollar, the international trade tomorrow, the Bundesbank meeting on Thursday, the situation among the Southeast Asian countries, the situation with the European Monetary Union," Harris also said.
Raymond Worseck, chief economist at AG Edwards and Sons, agreed that the absence of a Fed move was "certainly not a negative for stocks. It's neutral to modestly positive."
"But every time you are looking at the stock valuation you have now, the market has difficulties going up, unless interest rates go lower," Worseck cautioned. "We'll have to wait and see."
Worseck said any new stock rally would have to be tied to non-Fed events -- short of an easing.
